newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. preaches deregulation gospel in Japan trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. preaches deregulation gospel in Japan trade.

text.p: The United States is again preaching the deregulation gospel as it pushes Japan to improve market access and ensure the economic growth needed to prevent its contentious trade surplus from surging.

"The second Clinton Administration will continue to push Japan to accelerate pro-competitive regulatory reform aimed at improving market access," Larry Greenwood, economic minister-counselor at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo, said on Thursday, adding that there were two key reasons to do so.
"First, regulations lie at the heart of our market access problem with Japan," Greenwood told a news conference.

"The second reason...is the important role regulatory reform plays in promoting sustainable, domestic demand-led economic growth, particularly significant given the severe constraints Japan faces in pursuing aggressive fiscal or monetary policy. Such growth is critical to correcting long-term trade imbalances between our two countries."

Two-way trade disputes stayed backstage for much of last year but appear to be coming back into the limelight amid signs that Japan's current account surplus could bulge again after halving since 1994.
Data released on Thursday showed Japan's current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- grew more than four-fold in January from a year before.
The monthly surplus surged to 150.7 billion yen ($1.24 billion) from 32.6 billion yen ($269 million) in January 1996.

Washington has signalled it is keeping close tabs on Japan's surplus and wants Tokyo to take whatever fiscal or other steps are needed to boost domestic growth and rein in the surplus. Japan, however, is keen to cut its budget deficit.

"Japan needs to maintain sustained domestic demand-led growth and needs to take steps to avoid a resurgence of the current account surplus," Greenwood said. "This is a basic area of agreement between the U.S. and Japan in the macro area."

Greenwood cited a long list of sectors in which the United States plans to keep pressing Japan to cut red tape and eliminate rules that Washington as well as domestic critics say hobble competition and dampen imports.

Telecommunications topped the list of targets, which also included ports practices -- which could be the subject of trade sanctions next month if the two sides fail to work out some agreement -- further deregulation of Japan's auto parts and car inspection system, and transport in general.
Greenwood praised Japan's proposed "Big Bang" plan to open financial markets by the year 2001 and trade officials' plans to reform the distribution system.

He was less impressed by the government's broad three-year deregulation programme, about to be updated for the final time later this month. "What started off as a relatively vigorous process...has slowed as ministries find themselves unable or unwilling to make the hard decisions," he said.

Despite Washington's deregulation drive, Greenwood said the United States was not trying to remake Japan in its own economic image. "I've always viewed trade as being like sex -- it's the difference between the partners that makes it interesting," he joked.
